newsitem.title: USA: Fed leaves U.S. rates unchanged, more of same seen.
newsitem.headline: Fed leaves U.S. rates unchanged, more of same seen.

text.p: Federal Reserve policy makers left interest rates unchanged at their meeting on Wednesday, an outcome markets had anticipated and which many economists say will recur at December's policy meeting.
The Fed ended its meeting with no policy announcement, the central bank's way of showing that there was no policy change.
With unanimity, Fed watchers had expected that the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the policy-making arm of the Fed, would keep rates exactly as they were.

That consensus formed after a steady stream of data on such phenomena as inflation, payroll growth and retail sales showed that U.S. economic growth slowed in the third quarter -- just as the Fed had counted on at its July and September meetings -- from a brisk 3.5 percent growth pace in the first half of the year.
The Commerce Department reported early this month that Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew 2.2 percent in the third quarter. And economists believe even that number eventually will be revised lower.
"The Fed wanted to get growth down and their wish came true," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.

Rupkey said the demand side of the economy had fallen off quite sharply. He said not only had that enabled the Fed to hold interest rates steady, but that it also portended a steady rate policy for the foreseeable future.

"In both the February and July Humphrey-Hawkins testimony," Rupkey noted, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan "pretty well laid it out that growth needed to slow to the long-run growth trend of 2.5 percent or lower."
The 2.5-percent rate is widely viewed as a sustainable, or non-inflationary, rate of growth for the U.S. economy.
"Until the economy begins to grow faster than that again, I can't see any reason for them to tighten," he said. "It may be a status quo policy for quite some time into the future."
"There wasn't any pressure on the Fed to tighten," said Steve Ricchuito, chief financial economist at BZW Securities.
Ricchuito wondered whether the Fed had altered its policy directive to a balanced one from the assymetrical instruction biased toward tightening it adopted at its September meeting.
"They could go back to a symmetrical directive, but that might not be the smart thing to do, especially if the fourth quarter turns out to be strong," said Ricchuito.
But besides the possible fine tuning of the directive, Ricchuito believes Fed policy is on hold for the time being.
"If they're ever going to change policy, it's probably several months away -- something closer to the end of the first quarter," he said.
Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston Inc., said he expects no policy change until the Federal Open Market Committee's meeting in February -- at the earliest.
"Indications are that economic growth is going into the non-inflationary target range of about two to 2.5 percent," said Youngdahl. "With that scenario, there really is no reason to change rates.
